entities.name: De Humani Corporis Fabrica
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Published in 1543 by Andreas Vesalius (1514–1564) — the same year as Copernicus's De Revolutionibus — De Humani Corporis Fabrica (On the Fabric of the Human Body) is the founding work of modern anatomy. Based on systematic human dissection performed by Vesalius himself at the University of Padua (breaking with the medieval practice of lecturing from Galen while a barber-surgeon performed the actual cutting), the Fabrica corrected over 200 errors in the 1,400-year-old anatomical authority of Galen (who had dissected only animals).

Its 700+ pages are illustrated with over 200 exquisite woodcut illustrations — anatomical figures posed theatrically against Italian landscapes — produced by artists from Titian's workshop in Venice. These illustrations, combining scientific accuracy with artistic beauty, set a new standard for scientific illustration that endured for centuries. Vesalius was only 28 years old when he published this revolutionary work.

The Fabrica's insistence on direct observation over ancient textual authority — see for yourself rather than trust Galen — embodied the empirical ethos of the Scientific Revolution.
